body.p: Claims 1-20 are pending. Claims 1-18 are rejected and claims 19-20 are allowable. Claims 1, 3-6, 9, 10, and 12-20 are amended. No new matter has been added.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 112

Claims 3 and 12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. §112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre- AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention. This rejection is respectfully traversed. However, to expedite the prosecution of the application, claims 3 and 12 are amended. As such, it is respectfully requested that the section 112 rejection of claims 3 and 12 be withdrawn.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 102
Claims 1, 10, and 17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(2) as being anticipated by Stanney (US 11,551,407 B1). This rejection is respectfully traversed.
It is respectfully submitted that Stanney does not disclose the recitations of claim 1. Stanney does not disclose:
training an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments and based on the input
data regarding the plurality of real-world environments; and applying the Al model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding the first user to determine
a type of the real-world environment

as is recited in claim 1. Rather, Stanney describes detecting audio of objects and background in a 2D video scene and substituting the audio with pre-stored audio. However, the audio is of the objects and the background in the video scene and is not "the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments", as is recited in claim 1. The video scene in Stanney from which the audio of objects and background is
detected is not "real-world environments" but a virtual environment. Figure 1 of Stanney is reproduced below.
The digital image processor 120 may include an object detector
122 that may use machine-learning algorithms and/or neural networks to detect one or more objects in each frame of the
2D video. The digital image processor 120 may classify the
body.h1: background environment image data of the 2D video scene.
body.p: Example, general background environments may include the
following classifications: rural, urban, forest, beach, state, city,
and country. The system 100 may select or recommend a pre- stored 3D scene environment which closely matches or
correlates to the classified background environment. Example
machine-learning algorithms and neural networks are described
below in relation to FIG. 9. The digital image processor 120 may include an object tagger 124 configured to label and tag
the detected object in the frame. The label and tagging function
may provide object localization. The label and tag may
represent image coordinates with the detected object in the 2D
frame. The image coordinates include the (x,y) pixel location(s)
in the 2D frame. The at least one processor may process the
audio of a detected object so that it may be tagged and labeled for association with the corresponding object. By way of non- limiting examples, the machine-learning algorithms may
identify and classify the detected audio content of a particular object in the 2D video into one of a plurality of audio types and
then allow the author to tag it with a particular entity. The
system 100 may be configured to substitute the tagged audio tag with a pre-stored simulated audio stored in memory. The
system 100 may process the audio to determine background
audio as well to supplement the 3D environment with classified
body.h1: background audio. For example, at a beach, classified
background audio may include the sound of moving water,
body.p: birds and light breeze. In a city, for example, classified
body.h1: background audio may include moving vehicles, horns, etc. In
body.p: some scenarios, the original 2D audio content may include
audio representative of a car crash. The system 100 may tag the
audio and substitute a pre-stored audio segment representative of simulated car crash audio for the sounds of the recorded car
crash.
(see column 4, line 50- column 5, line 9)
(Emphasis added).

As such, in Stanney, the audio is of the detected object in the video scene, and not "generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments". Comparatively, the artificial intelligence model is trained "based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments". There is no such training, in Stanney, of the AI model "based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments". Rather, in Stanney, an audio of an object in a video scene is detected and substituted with recorded audio (Emphasis Added). Hence, Stanney fails to disclose "training an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments" and "applying the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding the first user to determine a type of the real-world environment", as is recited in claim 1. Thus, claim 1 submitted be novel in view of Stanney.
Also, claim 10 is submitted to be novel over Stanney. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, Stanney fails to disclose:
a processor configured to:

train an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments and based on the input data regarding the plurality of real- world environments; and

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine a type of the real-world environment as is recited in claim 10. Thus, claim 10 is submitted be novel in view of Stanney.
Moreover, claim 17 is submitted to be novel over Stanney. As an example, for the same reasons set forth above, Stanney fails to disclose: a server configured to:

train an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments and based on the input data regarding the plurality of real- world environments; and

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine a type of the real-world environment as is recited in claim 17. Thus, claim 17 is submitted be novel in view of Stanney.
Therefore, it is respectfully submitted that the section 102 rejection of claims 1, 10,
and 17 be withdrawn.
First Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 103
Claims 2 and 11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. f 103 as being unpatentable over Stanney and further in view of Chien (US 2023/0147573). This rejection is respectfully traversed.
Claim 2 depends from independent claim 1 and claim 11 depends from independent claim 10. It is respectfully submitted that the combination of Stanney and Chien does not
disclose or suggest the recitations of claim 1. For example, the combination of Stanney and Chien fails to teach:
training an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments and based on the input
data regarding the plurality of real-world environments; and applying the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding the first user to determine
a type of the real-world environment as is recited in claim 1.
As another example, the combination of Stanney and Chien fails to teach:
a processor configured to:

train an artificial intelligence (AI) model based on the plurality of sets of audio data generated from the sounds in the plurality of real-world environments and based on the input data regarding the plurality of real- world environments; and
apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine a type of the real-world environment

as is recited in claim 10. Stanney is explained above. Moreover, Chien is not cited to cure the deficiencies in Stanney. Rather, Chien is cited to disclose "extracted audio features from one or more representative audio samples, such as low-level audio features, including: spectral centroid, spectral roll-off, signal energy, mel-frequency cepstrum coefficients (MFCCs), linear predictor coefficients (LPC), line spectral frequency (LSF) coefficients, loudness coefficients, sharpness of loudness coefficients, spread of loudness coefficients, octave band signal intensities" (see Office Action, page 7). Hence, for the reasons set forth above, the independent claims 1 and 10 and the respective dependent claims 2 and 11 are submitted to be nonobvious in view of the combination of Stanney and Chien.
Therefore, it is respectfully requested that the section 103 rejection of claims 2 and 11 be withdrawn.
